analysis.one_liner: Sets a negligible-risk health standard for pesticide residues in food, forcing many to be banned or cut.
analysis.headline: The Senate committee approved the bill but the Senate never voted on it, and it died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the rules the EPA uses to decide how much pesticide residue is allowed on food. Every residue would have to meet a 'negligible risk' health standard, accounting for all sources of exposure over a lifetime, with special attention to infants and children. Existing tolerances would be re-reviewed, food would be tested for compliance, and pesticide makers would pay fees to fund the reviews. The bill was reported favorably out of committee but never came to a vote on the Senate floor before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Food consumers, especially infants and children, who would get tighter, health-based limits on pesticide residues in what they eat, plus stronger FDA testing and public access to the safety data behind pesticide approvals.

how_it_helps.text: A pesticide residue would be deemed unsafe unless a tolerance is in effect, and a tolerance could only stand if the risk from dietary exposure is negligible, counting all other sources of exposure, including drinking water, over a lifetime.
The EPA would have to evaluate risk separately for infants, toddlers, and other children's age groups rather than the population as a whole.
Residues that cause cancer in animals or humans could only be tolerated if lifetime risk stayed at or below one in a million using conservative risk models.

The EPA would have to re-evaluate every existing tolerance within set deadlines, revoke any based on inadequate data, and revoke tolerances that lack a reliable detection method, with public access to the data supporting petitions.
The FDA would conduct surveillance and compliance sampling of food for residues, and companies would pay fees to fund the review and testing programs.

analysis.who_pays: Pesticide manufacturers, who would lose tolerances for products that cannot meet the health standard and would pay fees for reviews and monitoring; growers and food processors, who could lose legal pesticide uses and face higher compliance costs, some of which would likely reach food prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill is deliberately strict: a one-in-a-million lifetime cancer risk standard and a 100-fold safety margin would force many existing tolerances to be lowered or revoked, which could remove useful pesticides from growers and raise production costs.
Pesticide makers would fund the system through fees, including annual fees just to keep a tolerance in effect, costs that tend to be passed along in food prices.
The re-review schedule gave the EPA up to seven years to work through all existing tolerances, meaning dangerous residues already in use could remain legal for years while data were gathered.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health gain — fewer carcinogenic and risky residues in food, with explicit protection for infants and children — is broad and lasting, while the costs fall on a concentrated industry and only partially pass into food prices. The main design criticism is the very conservative risk standard, which some would call overcautious, and the slow multi-year phase-in for old tolerances.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate's Labor and Human Resources committee approved it favorably in November 1991, but the Senate never brought it to the floor, and it died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Kennedy introduced the bill on May 14, 1991, with Sen. Christopher Dodd as the only cosponsor.
It was referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources, which asked the FDA and EPA for their views.
The committee held hearings on July 10, 1991.
On November 14, 1991, the committee ordered the bill to be reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute.
No further action was taken, and the bill never received a vote in the Senate before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pesticide manufacturers and agricultural users were better off: the stricter health standard, tolerance revocations, and fees never took effect, and pesticide residue rules stayed under the older, weaker framework.

for.name: Sen. Edward M. Kennedy
for.role: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; chair, Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and, as committee chair, moved it through hearings and a favorable committee report.

for.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
for.what_they_did: Held hearings, requested FDA and EPA comment, and ordered the bill reported favorably with a substitute amendment.

against.name: Pesticide manufacturers and agricultural and food industry groups
against.what_they_did: Faced stricter residue standards, tolerance revocations, and fees; the broader industry opposed the strict negligible-risk approach during the multi-year Delaney-clause pesticide debate.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate floor vote after the committee reported it favorably.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were Democrats and no floor vote was ever taken, so the record shows no partisan split on the merits.

industries.note: The bill would force re-review of every tolerance under a strict negligible-risk standard, revoking tolerances for residues that cannot meet it, and would impose fees including annual fees to keep tolerances in effect. Its interest in stopping the bill ran against consumers' interest in lower residues.

Stricter tolerances could remove legally usable pesticides and raise input costs, though residues posing negligible risk would remain permitted. Consumers would gain safer food; growers would bear compliance costs.
Processed-food tolerances would have to be set at the lowest level achievable under good manufacturing practice, and the industry would face residue-related liability if standards tightened.
